foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.sc: A labelled karyotype chart is displayed showing 47 chromosomes with an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). A brief clinical note states: newborn with hypotonia, single palmar crease, and upslanting palpebral fissures.
tk: Identify the total chromosome number shown and state whether it is normal or abnormal.
Name the chromosomal abnormality demonstrated.
State the most likely mechanism by which this abnormality arises during gametogenesis.
List two other clinical features you would look for to support this diagnosis.
ck: Correctly counts/states 47 chromosomes
Identifies trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
States meiotic non-disjunction as the mechanism
Mentions maternal age as a risk factor
Lists two plausible associated features (e.g., simian crease, epicanthic folds, cardiac defect)

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.sc: An electron micrograph shows a cell with an unusually extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum and a prominent Golgi apparatus.
tk: Identify the two organelles indicated by the arrows.
State the primary function of each organelle.
Predict the type of cell this is likely to be, based on organelle prominence.
Explain how the two organelles work together in protein processing.
ck: Correctly identifies rough ER and Golgi apparatus
States rough ER synthesizes/processes secretory and membrane proteins
States Golgi modifies, sorts, and packages proteins
Suggests a secretory cell (e.g., plasma cell, pancreatic acinar cell)
Describes the sequence: ribosome to rough ER to Golgi to vesicle

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.sc: A three-generation pedigree is shown in which an X-linked recessive condition affects only males, with carrier females in between, and no father-to-son transmission.
tk: State the mode of inheritance demonstrated by this pedigree.
Explain why the condition never passes from an affected father to his sons.
Calculate the risk to a son of a known carrier female.
Give one example of a real X-linked recessive disorder.
ck: Identifies X-linked recessive inheritance
Explains sons receive Y chromosome from father, not X
States 50% risk for sons of a carrier mother
Gives a valid example (e.g., hemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, red-green color blindness)

foundation/cell-biology-and-genetics.sc: Two labelled diagrams are shown side by side: one depicting a dividing somatic cell producing two identical daughter cells, and another depicting a germ cell producing four non-identical haploid cells.
tk: Identify which diagram represents mitosis and which represents meiosis.
State the chromosome number of the daughter cells in each process relative to the parent cell.
Name one event unique to meiosis that increases genetic variation.
State the biological purpose of each process.
ck: Correctly labels mitosis and meiosis diagrams
States mitosis daughter cells are diploid, meiosis products are haploid
Names crossing-over or independent assortment as a source of variation
States mitosis is for growth/repair, meiosis is for gamete formation

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.sc: A graph of reaction velocity against substrate concentration is displayed, showing a hyperbolic curve that plateaus at a maximum velocity (Vmax), with a second dashed curve reaching the same Vmax at a higher substrate concentration.
tk: Label the Vmax and Km on the graph.
Identify what type of enzyme inhibition the dashed curve most likely represents.
Explain, in terms of Km, why the dashed curve requires more substrate to reach half-maximal velocity.
State one clinical or biochemical example of this type of inhibition.
ck: Correctly labels Vmax and Km
Identifies competitive inhibition (same Vmax, increased Km)
Explains competitive inhibitor competes with substrate at active site
Gives a valid example (e.g., statins and HMG-CoA reductase, methotrexate and dihydrofolate reductase)

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.sc: A schematic of the inner mitochondrial membrane is shown with four numbered protein complexes and ATP synthase, with an arrow showing proton flow.
tk: Name Complex I through IV shown in the diagram.
State which complex is bypassed when FADH2 (rather than NADH) donates electrons.
Explain the chemiosmotic mechanism by which ATP synthase generates ATP.
Name one poison that blocks Complex IV and describe the consequence.
ck: Correctly names Complexes I-IV (NADH dehydrogenase, succinate dehydrogenase, cytochrome bc1, cytochrome c oxidase)
States FADH2 enters at Complex II, bypassing Complex I
Explains proton gradient driving ATP synthase (chemiosmosis)
Names cyanide or carbon monoxide blocking Complex IV, halting oxidative phosphorylation

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.sc: A simplified glycolysis pathway chart is shown from glucose to pyruvate, with two steps marked as irreversible/rate-limiting with a star.
tk: Identify the enzyme catalyzing the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis.
State the net ATP yield per glucose molecule from glycolysis alone.
Explain what happens to pyruvate under anaerobic conditions in skeletal muscle.
Name the allosteric activator and inhibitor of the rate-limiting enzyme.
ck: Identifies phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) as rate-limiting enzyme
States net yield of 2 ATP per glucose
States pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase under anaerobic conditions
Names AMP/fructose-2,6-bisphosphate as activators and ATP/citrate as inhibitors

foundation/bioenergetics-and-enzymes.sc: A double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot is shown with two lines: one representing an uninhibited enzyme reaction and another representing the same reaction with an inhibitor present, sharing the same x-intercept but different y-intercepts.
tk: State what the shared x-intercept indicates about Km in both conditions.
State what the different y-intercepts indicate about Vmax.
Identify the type of inhibition shown.
Give one biochemical example of this inhibition type.
ck: Recognizes unchanged x-intercept means unchanged Km
Recognizes different y-intercept (1/Vmax) means decreased Vmax with inhibitor
Identifies non-competitive inhibition
Gives a plausible example (e.g., heavy metal ion inhibition of an enzyme)

foundation/general-histology.sc: A photomicrograph shows a single layer of tall, narrow cells with basally located nuclei lining a tubular lumen, with a brush border visible on the apical surface.
tk: Identify the type of epithelium shown.
Name one organ location where this epithelium is typically found.
State the functional significance of the apical brush border.
State whether this epithelium is classified as simple or stratified, and why.
ck: Identifies simple columnar epithelium with microvilli (brush border)
Names a correct location (e.g., small intestine, gallbladder)
States brush border increases surface area for absorption
Correctly classifies as simple (one cell layer)

foundation/general-histology.sc: A photomicrograph shows chondrocytes sitting in lacunae within a glassy, homogeneous extracellular matrix, surrounded by a fibrous perichondrium.
tk: Identify the type of cartilage shown.
Name two locations in the body where this cartilage type is found.
Explain why cartilage heals slowly compared to bone.
Name the cells responsible for producing the cartilage matrix.
ck: Identifies hyaline cartilage
Names two correct locations (e.g., articular surfaces, costal cartilage, trachea, nasal septum)
States cartilage is avascular, limiting nutrient/oxygen delivery and repair
Names chondrocytes/chondroblasts as matrix-producing cells

foundation/general-histology.sc: A photomicrograph shows long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibers with peripherally located nuclei and clearly visible cross-striations running the length of the fiber.
tk: Identify the muscle type shown.
State whether this muscle type is under voluntary or involuntary control.
Explain the structural basis of the striations seen microscopically.
Contrast the nuclear position in this tissue with that of cardiac muscle.
ck: Identifies skeletal muscle
States it is voluntary, somatically innervated
Explains striations arise from the regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments (sarcomeres)
Notes cardiac muscle nuclei are typically central, single, with intercalated discs

foundation/general-histology.sc: A cross-sectional photomicrograph shows multiple axons, each surrounded by a myelin sheath, grouped into fascicles bound by a connective tissue layer.
tk: Name the connective tissue layers surrounding an individual axon, a fascicle, and the whole nerve.
Identify the cell type responsible for myelination in this tissue.
State the functional consequence of myelination on conduction velocity.
State one clinical condition caused by demyelination of peripheral nerves.
ck: Correctly names endoneurium (axon), perineurium (fascicle), epineurium (whole nerve)
Identifies Schwann cells as the myelinating cell of the PNS
States myelination increases conduction velocity (saltatory conduction)
Names a valid example (e.g., Guillain-Barre syndrome)

foundation/general-embryology.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of a trilaminar embryonic disc is shown with three labelled germ layers and the primitive streak indicated at one end.
tk: Name the three germ layers from outermost to innermost.
State the process by which the trilaminar disc forms from the bilaminar disc.
Name one adult derivative of each germ layer.
State the approximate gestational week at which gastrulation occurs.
ck: Correctly names ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm in order
Names gastrulation as the process, involving migration through the primitive streak
Gives a correct derivative for each layer (e.g., skin/CNS from ectoderm, muscle/bone from mesoderm, gut lining from endoderm)
States gastrulation occurs in week 3

foundation/general-embryology.sc: A diagram shows a lumbosacral defect with a fluid-filled sac containing meninges and spinal cord tissue protruding through a vertebral defect, labelled as a neural tube defect.
tk: Identify the specific defect shown (as opposed to meningocele without neural tissue).
Name the embryological process that fails to occur properly, producing this defect.
State one maternal supplement known to reduce the risk of neural tube defects.
Name the approximate week of development when neural tube closure normally completes.
ck: Identifies myelomeningocele (spina bifida cystica with neural tissue)
States failure of neural tube closure (neurulation)
Names folic acid supplementation
States neural tube closure completes by approximately week 4

foundation/general-embryology.sc: A labelled diagram of the placenta shows chorionic villi bathed in maternal blood within the intervillous space, with fetal capillaries inside the villi.
tk: Name the fetal and maternal components of the placenta shown.
List the layers separating fetal and maternal blood at term.
State one substance that crosses the placenta by simple diffusion.
Name one hormone produced by the placenta and its function.
ck: Identifies chorion frondosum (fetal) and decidua basalis (maternal)
Lists reduced barrier layers at term (syncytiotrophoblast, basement membrane, fetal endothelium)
Gives correct diffusing substance (e.g., oxygen, carbon dioxide)
Names a correct hormone (e.g., hCG maintaining corpus luteum, or hPL affecting maternal metabolism)

foundation/general-embryology.sc: Two diagrams are shown: one depicting dizygotic twins with two separate placentas and chorions, and another depicting monozygotic twins sharing a single placenta and chorion but with separate amnions.
tk: Identify the type of twinning in each diagram.
State the timing of embryo splitting that produces monochorionic-diamniotic monozygotic twins.
Explain why dizygotic twins are genetically no more similar than regular siblings.
Name one complication specific to monochorionic twin pregnancies.
ck: Correctly distinguishes dizygotic vs monozygotic twinning
States splitting between days 4-8 produces monochorionic-diamniotic twins
Explains dizygotic twins arise from two separate ova fertilized by two sperm
Names a valid complication (e.g., twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome)

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.sc: An epidemic curve (histogram of case counts against date of onset) is displayed showing a single sharp peak followed by a rapid decline, all cases occurring within one incubation period.
tk: Identify the pattern of epidemic curve shown.
State the most likely type of source (common-source vs propagated).
Suggest one appropriate immediate public health action.
State one piece of information you would need to identify the causative exposure.
ck: Identifies a point-source (common-source) epidemic curve
States single exposure to a common source, not person-to-person spread
Suggests a reasonable action (e.g., identify and remove the common source, such as contaminated food/water)
Requests relevant exposure history (e.g., food consumed, water source, gathering attended)

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.sc: A completed 2x2 table is shown comparing a screening test result (positive/negative) against true disease status (present/absent), with cell values filled in: true positive, false positive, false negative, true negative.
tk: Calculate the sensitivity of the test from the given values.
Calculate the specificity of the test from the given values.
State what a high sensitivity implies about the test's usefulness for screening.
State the formula used for positive predictive value.
ck: Correctly calculates sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN)
Correctly calculates specificity = TN/(TN+FP)
States high sensitivity means few false negatives, good for ruling out disease/screening
States PPV = TP/(TP+FP)

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.sc: A bell-shaped normal distribution curve is shown with the mean marked at the center and vertical lines marking one and two standard deviations on either side.
tk: State the approximate percentage of values falling within one standard deviation of the mean.
State the approximate percentage of values falling within two standard deviations of the mean.
Explain the relationship between mean, median, and mode in a perfectly normal distribution.
State one example of a biological variable that is approximately normally distributed.
ck: States approximately 68% within one SD
States approximately 95% within two SD
States mean = median = mode in a normal distribution
Gives a valid biological example (e.g., adult height, birth weight)

foundation/community-medicine-and-biosta.sc: A national immunization schedule chart is shown listing vaccines given at birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks, with one vaccine's column left blank for the candidate to fill in.
tk: Identify the vaccine missing from the blank column, based on the standard schedule.
State the route of administration typically used for BCG vaccine.
Explain the concept of herd immunity in relation to immunization coverage.
State one contraindication to giving a live attenuated vaccine.
ck: Correctly identifies the missing scheduled vaccine
States BCG is given intradermally
Explains herd immunity as indirect protection of unvaccinated individuals when coverage is high
States a valid contraindication (e.g., immunocompromised state, pregnancy)

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.t: Peripheral Blood Film - Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia
blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.sc: A peripheral blood film is displayed showing small red cells with a widened area of central pallor, along with occasional pencil-shaped cells. A brief note states: Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL.
tk: Describe the red cell morphology shown in descriptive terms.
Classify this anemia by MCV and state the likely category.
Name the single most useful confirmatory blood test to order next.
Name two common causes of this red cell picture.
ck: Describes microcytic, hypochromic cells with pencil cells
Classifies as microcytic anemia
Names serum ferritin/iron studies as confirmatory test
Names two valid causes (e.g., chronic blood loss, dietary iron deficiency, thalassemia trait)

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.sc: A labelled diagram shows the sequential stages of red cell maturation from proerythroblast to mature erythrocyte, with one intermediate stage left unlabeled.
tk: Name the unlabeled intermediate stage of erythropoiesis.
State the key nuclear change that occurs from proerythroblast to reticulocyte.
Name the principal hormone stimulating this process and its site of production.
State the normal reticulocyte percentage in peripheral blood.
ck: Correctly names the missing stage (e.g., normoblast/reticulocyte depending on diagram position)
States progressive nuclear condensation and eventual extrusion
Names erythropoietin, produced mainly by the kidney
States normal reticulocyte count approximately 0.5-1.5%

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.sc: A standard oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is shown with a dashed curve shifted to the right of the normal sigmoid curve.
tk: State whether the shifted curve represents increased or decreased hemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
List two physiological conditions that would cause this rightward shift.
Explain the functional benefit of a rightward shift at the tissue level.
Name the effect on P50 caused by this shift.
ck: States rightward shift means decreased oxygen affinity
Lists two valid causes (e.g., increased CO2, decreased pH, increased temperature, increased 2,3-BPG)
Explains easier oxygen unloading/release at tissues
States P50 increases with a rightward shift

blood/hematopoiesis-and-rbc-physiology.sc: A laboratory report shows a reticulocyte count of 6% with a hematocrit of 20% (reference hematocrit 45%), in a patient recovering from acute blood loss.
tk: Calculate the corrected reticulocyte count using the given values.
Interpret whether the marrow response is adequate or inadequate.
State what an inadequate reticulocyte response would suggest about marrow function.
Name the time after acute blood loss at which reticulocytosis typically peaks.
ck: Correctly calculates corrected count = 6 x (20/45) ≈ 2.7%
Interprets result correctly relative to expected response (adequate response typically >3%, so this borderline/slightly reduced)
States inadequate response suggests marrow suppression or nutrient deficiency
States reticulocytosis typically peaks around 5-10 days post-hemorrhage

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.t: Peripheral Blood Film - Neutrophilia with Left Shift
blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.sc: A peripheral blood film is shown with increased numbers of segmented neutrophils and several band forms, in a patient with fever and a raised total leukocyte count.
tk: Describe the abnormality shown on the film.
Define the term 'left shift' as used in hematology.
State the most likely underlying cause given the clinical context.
Name one other laboratory marker that would support acute bacterial infection.
ck: Describes neutrophilia with band forms (immature neutrophils)
Correctly defines left shift as increased immature neutrophil precursors in circulation
States acute bacterial infection as the most likely cause
Names a valid supporting marker (e.g., raised CRP, raised ESR, toxic granulation)

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.sc: A labelled Y-shaped immunoglobulin diagram is shown with heavy and light chains, variable and constant regions, and the Fc portion indicated.
tk: Label the antigen-binding site on the diagram.
Name the immunoglobulin class that crosses the placenta.
Name the immunoglobulin class found in secretions such as saliva and breast milk.
State the function of the Fc region.
ck: Correctly identifies the Fab/variable region as the antigen-binding site
Names IgG as the placenta-crossing class
Names IgA as the secretory class
States Fc region mediates effector functions (complement activation, binding to Fc receptors on immune cells)

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.sc: A simplified diagram of the complement system is shown depicting the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways converging on a common terminal pathway forming the membrane attack complex.
tk: Name the complement component that activates the classical pathway.
Name the complement component at which all three pathways converge.
State the function of the membrane attack complex.
Name one complement fragment that acts as an anaphylatoxin.
ck: Names C1q binding antigen-antibody complex as classical pathway trigger
Correctly identifies C3 as the convergence point
States MAC creates pores causing cell lysis
Names C3a or C5a as anaphylatoxins

blood/wbc-physiology-and-immunity.sc: A clinical vignette card describes a child developing wheezing, urticaria, and facial swelling within minutes of eating peanuts.
tk: Classify this reaction according to the Gell and Coombs classification.
Name the antibody class primarily responsible for this reaction.
Name the key effector cell involved in mediating the immediate reaction.
Name one mediator released that is responsible for the clinical features.
ck: Classifies as Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity
Names IgE as the responsible antibody
Names mast cells (or basophils) as the effector cell
Names a valid mediator (e.g., histamine, leukotrienes)

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.sc: A diagram of the coagulation cascade is shown with the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converging on a common pathway, with the initiating factor of the extrinsic pathway left blank.
tk: Name the initiating factor of the extrinsic pathway.
Name the laboratory test that primarily screens the extrinsic and common pathways.
Name the laboratory test that primarily screens the intrinsic and common pathways.
State the final common step shared by both pathways.
ck: Correctly names tissue factor (Factor III) as extrinsic pathway initiator
Names prothrombin time (PT) for extrinsic/common pathway
Names activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) for intrinsic/common pathway
States conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin via thrombin as the final common step

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.sc: A sequential diagram shows platelets adhering to exposed subendothelial collagen, then changing shape and aggregating to form a platelet plug at a site of vessel injury.
tk: Name the plasma protein that mediates platelet adhesion to collagen.
Name the platelet surface receptor involved in this adhesion step.
Name the substance released by activated platelets that promotes aggregation of further platelets.
Name the receptor responsible for platelet-to-platelet aggregation via fibrinogen bridging.
ck: Names von Willebrand factor as the adhesion mediator
Names GPIb receptor for adhesion
Names ADP or thromboxane A2 as an aggregation promoter
Names GPIIb/IIIa receptor for aggregation

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.sc: A laboratory report card shows: prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count, normal bleeding time, in a young male with recurrent hemarthroses.
tk: Interpret the pattern of results shown.
Name the most likely diagnosis given the clinical and laboratory picture.
Name the specific factor deficiency most commonly responsible for this presentation.
State the mode of inheritance of this condition.
ck: Correctly interprets isolated aPTT prolongation with normal PT and platelets
Names hemophilia as most likely diagnosis
Names Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) as most common
States X-linked recessive inheritance

blood/hemostasis-and-coagulation.sc: A diagram shows plasminogen being converted to plasmin, which then acts on a fibrin clot, releasing degradation products.
tk: Name the physiological activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin.
Name the fibrin degradation product commonly measured clinically to assess clot breakdown.
State one clinical condition in which this marker is characteristically elevated.
Name one drug that works by promoting this pathway.
ck: Names tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) as the physiological activator
Names D-dimer as the measured degradation product
Names a valid condition (e.g., deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, disseminated intravascular coagulation)
Names a thrombolytic drug (e.g., streptokinase, alteplase)

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.sc: A slide agglutination test is shown with a blood sample mixed separately with anti-A and anti-B sera: agglutination is seen with anti-A serum only, no agglutination with anti-B serum.
tk: State the ABO blood group of this sample based on the reactions shown.
Name the antigen present on the red cells of this individual.
Name the antibody or antibodies expected to be present in this individual's plasma.
State which donor blood groups could safely be transfused to this individual in an emergency, ABO-wise.
ck: Correctly identifies blood group A
States A antigen is present on red cells
States anti-B antibody present in plasma
States group A or group O blood could be given (O as universal donor)

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.sc: A diagram illustrates an Rh-negative mother sensitized during a first pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, followed by a second Rh-positive pregnancy showing maternal antibodies crossing the placenta.
tk: Name the condition affecting the fetus/newborn in the second pregnancy.
Explain the mechanism of maternal sensitization during the first pregnancy.
Name the class of antibody responsible for crossing the placenta and causing fetal hemolysis.
Name the prophylactic injection given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent this condition.
ck: Names hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis)
Explains fetomaternal hemorrhage exposing mother to Rh-positive fetal cells, producing anti-D antibodies
Names IgG as the placenta-crossing antibody class
Names anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) as prophylaxis

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.sc: A peripheral blood film shows large oval red cells and a hypersegmented neutrophil with six or more nuclear lobes, in a patient with glossitis and paresthesia.
tk: Describe the key morphological findings shown.
Classify this anemia by MCV.
Name the two vitamin deficiencies most commonly responsible for this picture.
Name the confirmatory investigation you would order to distinguish between the two.
ck: Describes macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils
Classifies as macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia
Names vitamin B12 and folate deficiency
Names serum B12 and folate levels (or Schilling test for B12) as confirmatory tests

blood/blood-groups-transfusion-and-anemi.sc: A peripheral blood film shows elongated, crescent-shaped red cells with pointed ends, along with target cells and occasional Howell-Jolly bodies.
tk: Identify the abnormal red cells shown and name the underlying condition.
State the genetic mutation responsible for this condition.
Explain why Howell-Jolly bodies may be seen on this film.
Name one precipitating factor that triggers a vaso-occlusive crisis.
ck: Identifies sickle cells and names sickle cell disease
States point mutation in the beta-globin gene (glutamic acid to valine substitution)
Explains Howell-Jolly bodies reflect functional hyposplenism/splenic infarction
Names a valid trigger (e.g., hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold exposure)

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.sc: A photomicrograph of a lymph node shows an outer cortex with germinal centers, a paracortex, and an inner medulla with medullary sinuses and cords.
tk: Identify the predominant lymphocyte type found in the cortical germinal centers.
Identify the predominant lymphocyte type found in the paracortex.
State the direction of lymph flow through the node, from afferent to efferent vessels.
Name the cells found in the medullary cords that produce antibodies.
ck: Identifies B lymphocytes in germinal centers
Identifies T lymphocytes in the paracortex
Describes flow: afferent lymphatics to subcapsular sinus to cortex/paracortex to medullary sinuses to efferent lymphatics
Names plasma cells as antibody-producing cells in medullary cords

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of the spleen is shown with regions labelled 'red pulp' and 'white pulp' around a central arteriole.
tk: State the main function of the red pulp.
State the main function of the white pulp.
Name the structure surrounding the central arteriole within the white pulp.
Name one clinical consequence of splenectomy relevant to infection risk.
ck: States red pulp filters and removes old/damaged red cells (splenic sequestration)
States white pulp is involved in immune response, containing lymphocytes
Names periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS)
States increased risk of infection with encapsulated organisms after splenectomy

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.sc: Two photomicrographs of thymic tissue are shown side by side: one from an infant with a densely cellular cortex and medulla, and another from an elderly adult showing marked replacement by fatty tissue.
tk: Name the process shown in the second (adult) image.
State the main function of the thymus during childhood.
Name the structure found in the thymic medulla used as a histological landmark.
Explain the clinical relevance of thymic involution to immune function with age.
ck: Names age-related thymic involution
States thymus is the site of T lymphocyte maturation/selection
Names Hassall's corpuscles as the medullary landmark
Explains reduced naive T cell output contributing to reduced immune competence with age

blood/lymphatic-system-anatomy-and-histo.sc: A diagram of the body's surface is shown with a marked lesion on the lateral aspect of the foot, and the candidate is asked to trace its lymphatic drainage.
tk: Name the first-order (primary) lymph node group draining this region.
Name the lymphatic trunk that ultimately receives drainage from the lower limb.
State which major vein this trunk drains into.
Explain the clinical significance of lymph node drainage patterns in the spread of infection or malignancy.
ck: Correctly names popliteal then superficial inguinal nodes as first-order drainage
Names the lumbar lymphatic trunk (via thoracic duct)
States drainage into the left subclavian vein (via thoracic duct) or right lymphatic duct as appropriate
Explains lymph nodes are common sites for spread of infection/metastasis following drainage pathways

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.sc: A labelled model/diagram of the brachial plexus is displayed with roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal branches, with one terminal branch left unlabeled arising from the posterior cord.
tk: Identify the unlabeled terminal branch arising from the posterior cord.
Name the root values contributing to this nerve.
Name one muscle group supplied by this nerve.
Describe the clinical deformity produced if this nerve is injured at the spiral groove of the humerus.
ck: Correctly identifies the radial nerve
Gives correct root values (C5-T1)
Names posterior arm/forearm extensor muscles
Describes wrist drop as the resulting deformity

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.sc: A dissected shoulder specimen/diagram shows four muscles surrounding the glenohumeral joint, forming the rotator cuff, with one muscle passing through the quadrangular space region left unlabeled.
tk: Name all four rotator cuff muscles.
Identify which one is most commonly torn clinically.
State the nerve supply of the muscle most commonly injured.
Describe the special clinical test used to assess this muscle's integrity.
ck: Correctly names supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
Identifies supraspinatus as most commonly torn
States suprascapular nerve as its supply
Describes the empty can (Jobe's) test or drop arm test

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the cubital fossa is shown with its boundaries outlined and three structures labelled from lateral to medial, with the middle structure left blank.
tk: Name the structure occupying the middle position (lateral to medial order).
Name the boundaries of the cubital fossa.
State the clinical significance of the biceps brachii tendon as a landmark during venipuncture.
Name the nerve that lies deep and medial, at risk during procedures in this region.
ck: Correctly identifies brachial artery as the middle structure (biceps tendon lateral, median nerve medial, or per standard 'TAN' order)
Names boundaries (brachioradialis laterally, pronator teres medially, imaginary line superiorly)
States tendon is a useful landmark protecting the brachial artery medially
Names median nerve as the medial, deeper structure at risk

musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.t: Carpal Bones and Median Nerve Compression
musculoskeletal-msk/upper-limb-anatomy.sc: A radiograph/diagram of the wrist shows the eight carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum forming the roof of the carpal tunnel, with the median nerve passing beneath it.
tk: Name the eight carpal bones in correct anatomical sequence.
Name the structures that pass through the carpal tunnel along with the median nerve.
Describe the sensory distribution affected in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Name one provocative clinical test used to diagnose this condition.
ck: Names carpal bones correctly (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate)
Names the flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons and flexor pollicis longus tendon
Describes sensory loss over lateral 3.5 digits palmar aspect
Names Tinel's sign or Phalen's test

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the femoral triangle is shown with its boundaries outlined and its contents labelled from lateral to medial, with the femoral canal left unlabeled at the medial end.
tk: Name the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial.
State what occupies the femoral canal and its clinical significance.
Name the boundaries of the femoral triangle.
Explain why femoral hernias are more common in women and typically present medial to the femoral vein.
ck: Correctly names order: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (NAVEL mnemonic)
States femoral canal contains lymphatics and is a potential site for femoral hernia
Names boundaries (inguinal ligament, sartorius, adductor longus)
Explains wider female pelvis and femoral canal predisposing to femoral hernia

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.t: Sciatic Nerve and Foot Drop Diagram
musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the posterior thigh shows the sciatic nerve dividing into two terminal branches near the popliteal fossa, with a clinical note describing a patient unable to dorsiflex the foot after a fibular neck fracture.
tk: Name the two terminal branches of the sciatic nerve.
Identify which branch is injured given the clinical scenario described.
Explain the anatomical basis for this nerve's vulnerability at the fibular neck.
Describe the resulting gait abnormality.
ck: Names tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves
Identifies common fibular nerve injury
Explains its superficial course winding around the fibular neck
Describes high-stepping (steppage) gait due to foot drop

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the hip joint is shown with the retinacular vessels and ligamentum teres artery supplying the femoral head, in the context of a displaced femoral neck fracture.
tk: Name the main arterial source supplying the femoral head in adults.
State the complication most feared after a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture.
Explain why the ligamentum teres artery contribution is often insufficient to prevent this complication in adults.
Name the artery from which the main blood supply to the femoral head arises.
ck: Names the medial circumflex femoral artery (via retinacular vessels) as the main source
States avascular necrosis of the femoral head as the feared complication
Explains ligamentum teres artery is often obliterated/insufficient in adults
Names the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery as origin of circumflex vessels

musculoskeletal-msk/lower-limb-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the lateral ankle is shown with three ligaments labelled, and a clinical vignette describes a patient with lateral ankle pain and swelling after an inversion injury.
tk: Name the three ligaments forming the lateral ligament complex of the ankle.
Identify which of these ligaments is most commonly injured in an inversion sprain.
State the mechanism of injury described in the vignette.
Name the special clinical test used to assess ankle ligament stability.
ck: Names anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior talofibular ligaments
Identifies anterior talofibular ligament as most commonly injured
States forced inversion (and plantarflexion) as the mechanism
Names the anterior drawer test

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.t: Vertebral Level Identification - Spinal Cord Termination
musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.sc: A midsagittal diagram of the vertebral column and spinal cord is shown, with the conus medullaris and cauda equina labelled, and lumbar puncture needle placement indicated at a specific level.
tk: State the vertebral level at which the spinal cord (conus medullaris) typically ends in an adult.
State the safe vertebral level range for performing a lumbar puncture and explain why it is safe.
Name the structures pierced by the needle as it passes from skin to subarachnoid space.
Explain why lumbar puncture can be safely performed below the level of cord termination.
ck: States spinal cord ends approximately at L1-L2 in adults
States L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace as the safe level
Names skin, fascia, supraspinous/interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, arachnoid
Explains cauda equina fibers float freely in CSF below cord termination, avoiding cord injury

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.sc: An isolated vertebra specimen/diagram is shown with a bifid spinous process, a triangular vertebral foramen, and foramina within the transverse processes.
tk: Identify the region of the vertebral column this vertebra belongs to.
Name the special foramina present in the transverse processes and state what passes through them.
Explain the significance of the bifid spinous process as an identifying feature.
Name a specific named vertebra in this region with atypical structure and describe one distinguishing feature.
ck: Identifies a cervical vertebra
Names foramen transversarium, transmitting vertebral artery and veins
States bifid spinous process is characteristic of C3-C6
Names atlas (C1, no body/spinous process) or axis (C2, has dens/odontoid process)

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of the spinal cord is shown with the corticospinal tract and dorsal columns highlighted on one side, and the spinothalamic tract highlighted on the other.
tk: State the function carried by the corticospinal tract.
State the function carried by the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
State the function carried by the spinothalamic tract.
Explain the level at which the spinothalamic tract fibers cross, in contrast to the dorsal columns.
ck: States corticospinal tract carries voluntary motor function
States dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration, and proprioception
States spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature
Explains spinothalamic fibers cross near their level of entry (within 1-2 segments), while dorsal column fibers cross in the medulla

musculoskeletal-msk/back-vertebral-colum.sc: A diagram shows a posterolateral herniation of the nucleus pulposus at the L4-L5 disc level, compressing an adjacent nerve root.
tk: Name the two components of the intervertebral disc shown.
Identify the nerve root most likely compressed by an L4-L5 posterolateral disc herniation.
State the clinical sign that would be positive on examination to suggest nerve root irritation.
State the typical direction of disc herniation and its anatomical explanation.
ck: Names nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus
Identifies L5 nerve root as typically affected
Names straight leg raise (SLR) test as a positive sign
Explains posterolateral herniation is favored due to a thinner posterior longitudinal ligament laterally

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.t: Long Bone Radiograph - Fracture Healing Stages
musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.sc: A series of radiographs is shown demonstrating sequential stages of fracture healing: hematoma formation, soft callus, hard callus, and remodeling.
tk: Name the four stages of fracture healing shown in correct order.
State the type of cartilage/bone tissue present in the soft callus stage.
Name the cells responsible for bone remodeling in the final stage.
State one systemic factor that can impair fracture healing.
ck: Correctly orders hematoma formation, soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus, hard (bony) callus, remodeling
States soft callus contains fibrocartilage
Names osteoclasts (resorption) and osteoblasts (formation) in remodeling
Names a valid impairing factor (e.g., poor blood supply, infection, smoking, diabetes, malnutrition)

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.sc: Diagrams of four different joints are shown: the shoulder, the elbow, the interphalangeal joint, and the wrist, each demonstrating a distinct type of movement.
tk: Classify each joint shown by its type of synovial joint (e.g., ball-and-socket, hinge).
Name the movement uniquely permitted at a ball-and-socket joint that is not permitted at a hinge joint.
Name the tissue lining the joint capsule that secretes synovial fluid.
State one function of synovial fluid.
ck: Correctly classifies shoulder as ball-and-socket, elbow/interphalangeal as hinge, wrist as condyloid
Names rotation (or circumduction) as unique to ball-and-socket joints
Names synovial membrane (synovium)
States a valid function (lubrication, nutrition of articular cartilage, shock absorption)

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.sc: A diagram shows the calcium homeostasis feedback loop involving the parathyroid gland, bone, kidney, and intestine, with one hormone's site of action left unlabeled.
tk: Name the hormone that raises serum calcium by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption.
Name the hormone that lowers serum calcium and its cell of origin.
State the effect of parathyroid hormone on renal calcium and phosphate handling.
Name the active form of vitamin D and its role in calcium homeostasis.
ck: Names parathyroid hormone (PTH) as increasing bone resorption
Names calcitonin, produced by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid
States PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption and decreases phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturic)
Names calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which increases intestinal calcium absorption

musculoskeletal-msk/bone-joint-and-carti.sc: Two radiographs are displayed side by side: one showing generalized reduced bone density with thinned cortices in an elderly patient, and another showing pseudofractures (Looser's zones) in a patient with chronic vitamin D deficiency.
tk: Identify the condition shown in each radiograph.
State the fundamental biochemical difference between the two conditions (mineralization vs bone mass).
Name the primary biochemical deficiency underlying the second condition.
Name one laboratory test that would help distinguish between the two conditions.
ck: Identifies osteoporosis (first) and osteomalacia (second, with Looser's zones)
States osteoporosis is reduced bone mass with normal mineralization; osteomalacia is defective mineralization of normal bone matrix
Names vitamin D deficiency as the underlying cause of osteomalacia
Names serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, or vitamin D levels as distinguishing tests

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.sc: A labelled sarcomere diagram is shown at rest, with A band, I band, H zone, and Z lines marked, alongside a second diagram of the same sarcomere in a contracted state.
tk: State which bands/zones shorten during contraction and which remains constant in length.
Name the two proteins that undergo cross-bridge cycling.
Name the ion that triggers cross-bridge cycling by binding to troponin.
State the immediate source of energy required for cross-bridge cycling.
ck: States I band and H zone shorten; A band length stays constant
Names actin and myosin
Names calcium ion (Ca2+)
States ATP as the immediate energy source

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.sc: A diagram of the neuromuscular junction is shown with a motor neuron terminal, synaptic cleft, and postsynaptic muscle membrane with receptors labelled.
tk: Name the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction.
Name the postsynaptic receptor type that binds this neurotransmitter.
Name the enzyme responsible for terminating neurotransmitter action in the synaptic cleft.
Name one disease caused by autoantibodies against the postsynaptic receptor.
ck: Names acetylcholine
Names nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Names acetylcholinesterase
Names myasthenia gravis

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.sc: A table/diagram compares two muscle fiber types across mitochondrial content, myoglobin content, capillary density, and predominant metabolism, with fiber type names left blank.
tk: Name the fiber type with high mitochondrial content, high myoglobin, and oxidative metabolism.
Name the fiber type with low mitochondrial content and predominant glycolytic metabolism.
State which fiber type fatigues more slowly and why.
Give one example of a muscle predominantly composed of each fiber type.
ck: Names Type I (slow oxidative) fibers correctly
Names Type II (fast glycolytic) fibers correctly
States Type I fibers fatigue more slowly due to reliance on aerobic metabolism and rich blood supply
Gives plausible examples (e.g., soleus for Type I, extraocular/extensor digitorum for Type II)

musculoskeletal-msk/muscle-physiology-an.sc: A laboratory report shows markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) levels in a patient presenting with muscle weakness and myalgia after starting a new medication.
tk: State the clinical significance of an elevated serum creatine kinase level.
Name one class of drug commonly associated with drug-induced muscle injury of this kind.
Name the serious complication of muscle breakdown that can affect the kidneys.
Name one other laboratory or urine finding that would support this complication.
ck: States elevated CK indicates muscle cell damage/breakdown (rhabdomyolysis or myopathy)
Names statins as a common causative drug class
Names acute kidney injury due to myoglobin-induced tubular damage
Names myoglobinuria (dark/tea-colored urine) or elevated serum myoglobin as supporting finding

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.t: Heart Chamber and Valve Model Station
cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.sc: A dissected heart specimen/model is displayed with the chambers opened, showing the atrioventricular and semilunar valves, with the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle left unlabeled.
tk: Name the valve located between the left atrium and left ventricle.
State the number of cusps this valve has.
Name the structures that prevent this valve from prolapsing into the atrium during ventricular systole.
Name the auscultation area on the chest wall where this valve is best heard.
ck: Correctly names mitral (bicuspid) valve
States it has two cusps
Names chordae tendineae attached to papillary muscles
Names the mitral area (5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line)

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.sc: An anterior view diagram of the heart is shown with the coronary arteries traced, and a marked occlusion in the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery.
tk: Name the region of myocardium supplied by the LAD artery.
State the ECG leads that would typically show changes with LAD occlusion (anterior wall).
Name the artery that supplies the SA node in most individuals.
State which coronary artery most commonly gives rise to the posterior descending artery, and what this determines.
ck: States LAD supplies the anterior interventricular septum and anterior wall of left ventricle
Names leads V1-V4 for anterior changes
Names right coronary artery (RCA) as the usual SA nodal supply
Explains right coronary dominance (RCA gives posterior descending artery in ~85%) determining coronary dominance

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.sc: A diagram of fetal circulation is shown with three shunts labelled: one between the umbilical vein and IVC, one between the right and left atria, and one between the pulmonary artery and aorta.
tk: Name the three fetal shunts shown.
State the postnatal structure each shunt becomes after closure.
Explain the physiological trigger for closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth.
Name the condition that results if the ductus arteriosus fails to close.
ck: Names ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus
States postnatal remnants: ligamentum venosum, fossa ovalis, ligamentum arteriosum
Explains rising oxygen tension and falling prostaglandin E levels trigger closure
Names patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)

cardiovascular-cvs/heart-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the heart's conducting system is shown with the SA node, AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers labelled, with the bundle branches left unlabeled.
tk: Name the structure connecting the bundle of His to the Purkinje fibers.
State the normal intrinsic firing rate of the SA node.
Explain the functional significance of the delay at the AV node.
Name the condition resulting from complete failure of AV conduction.
ck: Names right and left bundle branches
States SA node fires at approximately 60-100 beats per minute
Explains AV delay allows completion of atrial contraction/ventricular filling before ventricular contraction
Names complete (third-degree) heart block

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.sc: A Wiggers diagram is shown displaying aortic pressure, ventricular pressure, atrial pressure, and the ECG, aligned in time, with the period of isovolumetric contraction marked with a question mark.
tk: Identify the phase marked on the diagram and define it.
State which two heart valves are closed during this phase.
Identify the heart sound generated at the start of this phase.
State what event marks the end of isovolumetric contraction.
ck: Correctly identifies isovolumetric contraction and defines it as ventricular contraction with all valves closed, no change in volume
States mitral and aortic valves are both closed during this phase
Identifies S1 (first heart sound) at the start
States aortic valve opening (when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure) ends this phase

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.sc: A graph is shown plotting stroke volume (or cardiac output) on the y-axis against left ventricular end-diastolic volume (preload) on the x-axis, with two curves: a normal curve and a curve shifted upward and to the left.
tk: State the physiological principle illustrated by the normal curve.
Identify what the upward-left shifted curve represents.
Name one physiological or pharmacological factor that could produce this shift.
Name one factor that would shift the curve downward and to the right.
ck: States the Frank-Starling law: increased preload increases stroke volume up to a limit
Identifies increased contractility
Names a valid positive inotrope (e.g., sympathetic stimulation, digoxin, calcium)
Names a valid negative factor (e.g., heart failure, negative inotropes, acidosis)

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.sc: A station is set up with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope on a mannequin arm, with a card describing the sequential Korotkoff sounds heard during cuff deflation.
tk: State which Korotkoff sound corresponds to systolic blood pressure.
State which Korotkoff sound (or event) corresponds to diastolic blood pressure.
Explain the physiological basis for the first Korotkoff sound appearing.
State the formula for calculating mean arterial pressure from systolic and diastolic pressure.
ck: States Korotkoff phase I (first sound) marks systolic pressure
States Korotkoff phase V (sound disappearance) marks diastolic pressure
Explains turbulent flow through the partially occluded artery generates the first sound
States MAP = diastolic pressure + 1/3(systolic - diastolic pressure)

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-physiology.sc: A flow diagram shows cardiac output as the product of heart rate and stroke volume, with stroke volume further broken down into preload, afterload, and contractility.
tk: State the normal formula for cardiac output.
Define afterload in physiological terms.
State the effect of increased afterload on stroke volume, all else being equal.
Name one clinical condition that chronically increases afterload on the left ventricle.
ck: States cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume
Defines afterload as the resistance/pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood
States increased afterload decreases stroke volume
Names a valid condition (e.g., systemic hypertension, aortic stenosis)

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.sc: A standard ECG tracing is displayed with the P wave, QRS complex, T wave, and PR and QT intervals shown, with the ST segment left unlabeled.
tk: Identify and label the ST segment on the tracing.
State the electrophysiological event represented by the ST segment.
State the normal duration range of the PR interval.
Name one condition that causes ST segment elevation.
ck: Correctly identifies the ST segment (end of QRS to start of T wave)
States it represents the plateau phase of ventricular depolarization/early repolarization (ventricles depolarized)
States normal PR interval is 0.12-0.20 seconds
Names a valid cause (e.g., acute myocardial infarction, pericarditis)

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.sc: An ECG rhythm strip is shown with an irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, and a fibrillatory baseline.
tk: Identify the arrhythmia shown.
State the main risk associated with this arrhythmia relevant to stroke prevention.
Name one class of drug used for rate control in this arrhythmia.
Explain why this rhythm is described as 'irregularly irregular'.
ck: Identifies atrial fibrillation
States risk of thromboembolism/stroke due to atrial stasis and clot formation
Names a valid rate-control drug class (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin)
Explains chaotic atrial activity produces a variable, unpredictable ventricular response

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.sc: A graph of the ventricular myocyte action potential is shown with five phases (0-4) labelled, with phase 2 (the plateau) highlighted.
tk: Name the ion primarily responsible for phase 0 (rapid depolarization).
Name the ion primarily responsible for maintaining the plateau in phase 2.
State the functional significance of the plateau phase in preventing tetany.
Name the ion movement responsible for phase 3 repolarization.
ck: Names sodium influx for phase 0
Names calcium influx (through L-type channels) for phase 2
Explains the plateau prolongs the refractory period, preventing sustained/tetanic contraction
Names potassium efflux for phase 3

cardiovascular-cvs/ecg-and-cardiac-elect.sc: An ECG is shown with ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.
tk: Identify the anatomical wall of the myocardium affected based on these lead changes.
Name the coronary artery most likely occluded, given this territory.
State one reciprocal ECG change that might be expected in this presentation.
Name the cardiac enzyme typically used to confirm myocardial infarction.
ck: Correctly identifies the inferior wall
Names the right coronary artery (RCA) as the usual culprit vessel
Names reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL
Names troponin as the confirmatory cardiac biomarker

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.sc: A flow diagram of the baroreceptor reflex is shown starting from carotid sinus/aortic arch stretch receptors, through the medulla, to efferent autonomic outputs, with one step left blank following a fall in blood pressure.
tk: Complete the reflex arc: state what happens to baroreceptor firing when blood pressure falls.
State the resulting change in sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow.
State the net effect on heart rate and vascular resistance.
Name the two main sites where baroreceptors are located.
ck: States decreased baroreceptor firing with falling blood pressure
States increased sympathetic outflow and decreased parasympathetic (vagal) outflow
States increased heart rate and increased peripheral vascular resistance, raising blood pressure back toward normal
Names carotid sinus and aortic arch

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.sc: A diagram of the RAAS pathway is shown from renin release through angiotensin I, angiotensin II, and aldosterone, with the site of ACE action left unlabeled.
tk: Name the organ/site where angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) primarily acts.
State the two main physiological actions of angiotensin II.
Name the site of aldosterone action and its main effect on sodium handling.
Name one class of antihypertensive drug that acts on this pathway.
ck: Names the pulmonary vascular endothelium (lungs) as the main site of ACE activity
States angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release
States aldosterone acts on the distal tubule/collecting duct to increase sodium (and water) reabsorption
Names ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.sc: A diagram of a capillary bed is shown with arrows depicting hydrostatic and oncotic pressures acting at the arterial and venous ends, with net fluid movement indicated.
tk: Name the two opposing forces that determine net fluid movement across the capillary wall.
State the direction of net fluid movement at the arterial end of the capillary and explain why.
State the direction of net fluid movement at the venous end and explain why.
Name one clinical condition that leads to edema through reduced plasma oncotic pressure.
ck: Names capillary hydrostatic pressure and plasma (colloid) oncotic pressure
States net filtration (fluid moves out) at arterial end where hydrostatic pressure dominates
States net absorption (fluid moves in) at venous end where oncotic pressure dominates
Names a valid condition (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, malnutrition)

cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.t: Peripheral Vascular Examination - Pulse Palpation Station
cardiovascular-cvs/vascular-physiology-a.sc: A mannequin limb is set up for pulse examination, with labelled anatomical landmarks for common palpation sites, and a clinical note describing a patient with suspected peripheral arterial disease.
tk: Name four peripheral pulse sites you would palpate in a lower limb vascular examination.
State what a weak or absent dorsalis pedis pulse combined with normal femoral pulse suggests about the level of arterial obstruction.
Name the bedside index used to objectively assess peripheral arterial disease severity.
State the components of this index's calculation.
ck: Names femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis pulses
Suggests obstruction distal to the femoral level (e.g., popliteal or below)
Names the ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI/ABI)
States it is ankle systolic pressure divided by brachial systolic pressure

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.sc: A photomicrograph of cardiac muscle is shown with branching fibers, centrally placed single nuclei, and dark-staining intercalated discs visible between adjacent cells.
tk: Identify the tissue type shown.
Name the structure responsible for electrical and mechanical coupling between adjacent cardiac muscle cells.
Name the two types of junctions found within this structure and their respective functions.
Explain how this structure allows the myocardium to function as a syncytium.
ck: Identifies cardiac muscle
Names intercalated discs
Names gap junctions (electrical coupling) and desmosomes/fascia adherens (mechanical coupling)
Explains gap junctions allow rapid ion flow enabling coordinated, wave-like contraction (functional syncytium)

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.sc: A sequence of diagrams shows the primitive heart tube undergoing looping, followed by septation into four chambers, with one stage of septal development left unlabeled.
tk: Name the embryological structure that gives rise to the primitive heart tube.
State the direction of normal cardiac looping.
Name the septum that initially divides the primitive atrium, leaving an interatrial communication.
Name the congenital defect that results from failure of atrial septation.
ck: Names the cardiogenic (primary heart) field/splanchnic mesoderm
States normal looping occurs to the right (dextral looping)
Names septum primum (with the ostium secundum/foramen ovale mechanism)
Names atrial septal defect (ASD)

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.sc: A graph is shown plotting serum concentration of cardiac biomarkers against time after onset of chest pain, with troponin and CK-MB curves plotted, one rising and remaining elevated for days, and the other rising and returning to baseline more quickly.
tk: Identify which curve represents troponin and which represents CK-MB.
State the approximate time troponin first becomes detectable after myocardial injury.
Explain why troponin is preferred over CK-MB as the primary biomarker for diagnosing myocardial infarction.
State one situation in which CK-MB remains clinically useful despite troponin's greater sensitivity.
ck: Correctly identifies the longer-elevated curve as troponin, the shorter as CK-MB
States troponin becomes detectable within approximately 3-6 hours
Explains troponin has higher cardiac specificity and remains elevated longer, improving diagnostic sensitivity
Names detecting reinfarction (since CK-MB normalizes faster and can show a new rise)

cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.t: Lipid Profile and Atherosclerosis Risk Station
cardiovascular-cvs/cardiac-histology-emb.sc: A laboratory lipid profile report is shown: total cholesterol elevated, LDL elevated, HDL low, triglycerides mildly elevated, in a patient being risk-stratified for cardiovascular disease.
tk: State which lipoprotein fraction is most directly implicated in atherogenesis.
State the role of HDL in lipid metabolism and why a low level is a risk factor.
Describe the initial step in atherosclerotic plaque formation involving LDL and the vessel wall.
Name one modifiable lifestyle factor that improves this lipid profile.
ck: Names LDL (low-density lipoprotein) as most atherogenic
States HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport, and low levels reduce this protective effect
Describes LDL oxidation/subendothelial deposition and uptake by macrophages forming foam cells
Names a valid factor (e.g., dietary modification, exercise, smoking cessation, weight loss)

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.sc: A resin cast/model of the bronchial tree is displayed showing the trachea dividing into main bronchi, then lobar and segmental bronchi, with the right lung's lobes and fissures labelled.
tk: State the number of lobes and bronchopulmonary segments in the right lung.
Explain why an inhaled foreign body is more likely to lodge in the right main bronchus than the left.
Name the fissures present in the right lung.
Define a bronchopulmonary segment and state its clinical/surgical significance.
ck: States right lung has 3 lobes and 10 bronchopulmonary segments
Explains right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left
Names oblique and horizontal fissures
Defines a segment as an independently resectable unit with its own segmental bronchus and artery

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the thoracic cavity in cross-section shows the parietal and visceral pleura, with the costodiaphragmatic recess indicated at the base of the pleural cavity.
tk: Name the structure being indicated (costodiaphragmatic recess) and describe its location.
State the clinical significance of this recess with respect to pleural effusion drainage.
Name the nerve supplying sensation to the parietal pleura lining the diaphragm centrally.
State the layer of pleura that is pain-sensitive.
ck: Correctly describes the costodiaphragmatic recess between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura
States it is the most dependent part of the pleural cavity where fluid tends to collect (site for thoracentesis)
Names the phrenic nerve for central diaphragmatic pleura
States parietal pleura is pain-sensitive; visceral pleura is not

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the larynx is shown with the thyroid, cricoid, and arytenoid cartilages labelled, along with the recurrent laryngeal and superior laryngeal nerves.
tk: Name the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway shown in this diagram.
Name the muscle responsible for tensing the vocal cords and its nerve supply.
State the effect of unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury on voice.
Name a common surgical procedure that risks injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
ck: Names the cricoid cartilage as the complete ring
Names cricothyroid muscle, supplied by external branch of superior laryngeal nerve
States hoarseness of voice with unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
Names thyroidectomy as a procedure placing this nerve at risk

respiratory/respiratory-system-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the diaphragm viewed from below is shown with three openings labelled at different vertebral levels, and the structures passing through each opening indicated with blanks.
tk: Name the three main openings in the diaphragm and their vertebral levels.
List the structures passing through the opening at T8.
List the structures passing through the opening at T10.
List the structures passing through the opening at T12.
ck: Names caval opening (T8), esophageal hiatus (T10), aortic hiatus (T12)
States IVC and right phrenic nerve pass through T8
States esophagus and vagal trunks pass through T10
States aorta, azygos vein, and thoracic duct pass through T12

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.sc: A spirometry graph (volume-time trace) is displayed showing tidal volume, and marked segments for inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume, with total lung capacity indicated.
tk: Label which lung volume cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry, and explain why.
Define vital capacity in terms of the component volumes shown.
State the normal approximate tidal volume in a resting adult.
Name one additional test needed to measure residual volume and total lung capacity.
ck: Identifies residual volume as unmeasurable by simple spirometry (since it cannot be exhaled)
Defines vital capacity = inspiratory reserve volume + tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume
States approximately 500 mL
Names helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.sc: Two flow-volume loops are shown: one with a scooped-out concave expiratory limb typical of obstructive disease, and one that is narrow with reduced volumes but preserved shape typical of restrictive disease.
tk: Identify which loop represents obstructive disease and which represents restrictive disease.
State the expected change in FEV1/FVC ratio in obstructive disease.
State the expected change in FEV1/FVC ratio in restrictive disease.
Name one example condition for each pattern.
ck: Correctly distinguishes the concave/scooped loop as obstructive and the narrow-but-normal-shaped loop as restrictive
States decreased FEV1/FVC ratio in obstructive disease
States normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio in restrictive disease
Gives valid examples (e.g., COPD/asthma for obstructive; pulmonary fibrosis for restrictive)

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.sc: A pressure-volume compliance curve of the lung is displayed, showing two curves: one representing normal lung compliance and a second curve shifted downward and to the right, representing reduced compliance.
tk: Define pulmonary compliance in physiological terms.
Identify what the downward-right shifted curve represents clinically.
Name one condition that causes decreased lung compliance.
Name one condition that causes increased lung compliance.
ck: Defines compliance as change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure
Identifies decreased compliance (stiffer lung)
Names a valid cause (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema)
Names a valid cause (e.g., emphysema, normal aging)

respiratory/pulmonary-ventilation-and-me.sc: A neonatal chest radiograph is shown with a diffuse ground-glass appearance and air bronchograms, accompanied by a clinical note of a premature infant with respiratory distress shortly after birth.
tk: Name the condition suggested by this clinical and radiological picture.
Name the cell type responsible for producing surfactant.
State the physiological role of surfactant in preventing alveolar collapse.
Name one antenatal intervention that reduces the risk of this condition.
ck: Names neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency)
Names type II pneumocytes
States surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing collapse (per Laplace's law) especially in small alveoli
Names antenatal corticosteroid administration to the mother

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.sc: An oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is displayed with a shift to the left compared to the normal curve, in the context of a blood gas sample showing alkalosis and hypothermia.
tk: State whether this leftward shift represents increased or decreased hemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
List two factors from the vignette that would produce this leftward shift.
Explain the functional consequence of a leftward shift at the level of peripheral tissues.
State the effect of fetal hemoglobin on the position of this curve compared to adult hemoglobin.
ck: States leftward shift means increased oxygen affinity
Identifies alkalosis (Bohr effect) and hypothermia as causes
Explains reduced oxygen unloading/release to tissues at a given partial pressure
States fetal hemoglobin has a left-shifted curve (higher affinity) compared to adult hemoglobin, facilitating placental oxygen transfer

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.sc: An electron micrograph/diagram of the alveolar-capillary (respiratory) membrane is shown with its component layers labelled, with the type of alveolar cell responsible for gas exchange left unlabeled.
tk: Name the alveolar cell type primarily responsible for gas exchange shown in this diagram.
List the layers of the respiratory membrane from alveolar air to capillary blood.
State the physical property of this membrane that facilitates rapid gas diffusion.
Name one disease process that thickens this membrane and impairs gas exchange.
ck: Names type I pneumocytes
Lists alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium (and surfactant layer)
States the membrane is extremely thin, maximizing diffusion per Fick's law
Names a valid condition (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, ARDS)

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.sc: A diagram shows three forms in which carbon dioxide is transported in the blood: dissolved CO2, carbaminohemoglobin, and bicarbonate, with proportions indicated by pie-chart segments.
tk: Name the predominant form in which CO2 is transported in the blood.
Name the enzyme responsible for converting CO2 and water into carbonic acid within red blood cells.
Describe the chloride shift and its physiological purpose.
State the term used for deoxygenated hemoglobin's increased ability to carry CO2 and H+.
ck: States bicarbonate is the predominant transport form (~70%)
Names carbonic anhydrase
Describes chloride ions moving into red cells in exchange for bicarbonate moving out, maintaining electrical neutrality
Names the Haldane effect

respiratory/gas-exchange-and-transport.sc: A diagram compares normal alveolar ventilation-perfusion matching to a region with V/Q mismatch, showing one alveolus that is ventilated but not perfused (dead space) and another that is perfused but not ventilated (shunt).
tk: State the approximate normal V/Q ratio for the lung as a whole.
Identify which labelled region represents dead space and which represents shunt.
State the effect of a pulmonary embolism on V/Q ratio in the affected segment.
State whether hypoxemia from a shunt is corrected by giving 100% oxygen, and explain why or why not.
ck: States normal V/Q ratio is approximately 0.8
Correctly identifies ventilated-not-perfused as dead space, perfused-not-ventilated as shunt
States pulmonary embolism increases V/Q ratio (ventilation without perfusion, dead space-like)
Explains shunt hypoxemia is not fully corrected by 100% oxygen since unventilated alveoli receive no oxygen to diffuse

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.sc: A diagram shows the medullary central chemoreceptors bathed in cerebrospinal fluid, responding to changes in CSF pH, with an arterial blood gas report showing elevated PaCO2.
tk: Explain how a rise in arterial PaCO2 leads to stimulation of central chemoreceptors.
State why central chemoreceptors respond to CSF hydrogen ion concentration rather than CO2 directly.
Name the primary site of the central chemoreceptors.
State the ventilatory response expected from a rise in PaCO2.
ck: Explains CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and combines with water to form carbonic acid, releasing H+ in the CSF
States CSF has poor buffering capacity, making pH highly sensitive to changes in dissolved CO2
Names the ventral medulla oblongata
States increased ventilation (rate and depth) in response to rising PaCO2

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.sc: A diagram shows the carotid and aortic bodies with their afferent nerve connections to the brainstem respiratory centers, alongside a clinical note of a patient with severe hypoxemia and a compensatory increase in ventilation.
tk: Name the primary stimulus detected by peripheral chemoreceptors that triggers this ventilatory response.
Name the nerves carrying afferent information from the carotid and aortic bodies respectively.
State at what approximate PaO2 threshold peripheral chemoreceptors become significantly activated.
Explain why peripheral chemoreceptors become the primary drive for ventilation in patients with chronic CO2 retention.
ck: Identifies low PaO2 (hypoxemia) as the primary peripheral chemoreceptor stimulus
Names glossopharyngeal nerve (carotid body) and vagus nerve (aortic body)
States significant activation occurs below approximately 60 mmHg PaO2
Explains chronic CO2 retention blunts central chemoreceptor sensitivity, making hypoxic drive via peripheral chemoreceptors more important

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.sc: A midsagittal brainstem diagram is shown with the dorsal respiratory group, ventral respiratory group, pneumotaxic center, and apneustic center labelled at their approximate locations.
tk: State the brainstem location of the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups.
State the primary function of the dorsal respiratory group.
State the function of the pneumotaxic center located in the pons.
Describe the effect on breathing pattern if the pneumotaxic center is removed experimentally.
ck: States both groups are located in the medulla oblongata
States dorsal respiratory group primarily controls the basic rhythm of inspiration
States pneumotaxic center limits inspiration duration, regulating respiratory rate/pattern
Describes apneustic breathing (prolonged inspiratory gasps) resulting from pneumotaxic center removal

respiratory/control-of-respiration-and-r.sc: A case vignette describes a trekker ascending rapidly to high altitude, developing hyperventilation and later showing an arterial blood gas with low PaO2, low PaCO2, and elevated pH.
tk: Explain the immediate ventilatory response to the hypoxia of high altitude.
Interpret the acid-base disturbance shown in the arterial blood gas.
Name the renal compensatory mechanism that occurs over subsequent days at altitude.
Name one hematological adaptation that develops with chronic altitude exposure.
ck: Explains hypoxia stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, increasing ventilation
Correctly interprets respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2, high pH) due to hyperventilation
Names increased renal bicarbonate excretion as compensation
Names increased erythropoietin secretion leading to polycythemia

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.sc: Two photomicrographs are shown side by side: one of a bronchus with cartilage plates and submucosal glands, and one of a bronchiole lacking cartilage but with a thicker relative smooth muscle layer.
tk: Identify which slide represents the bronchus and which represents the bronchiole.
State the key histological feature that distinguishes bronchi from bronchioles.
Explain the functional significance of the smooth muscle layer in bronchioles regarding airway resistance.
Name the type of epithelium lining the terminal bronchioles.
ck: Correctly identifies the cartilage/gland-containing slide as bronchus, the other as bronchiole
States absence of cartilage and glands in bronchioles is the key distinguishing feature
Explains smooth muscle tone/bronchoconstriction directly regulates airway resistance in bronchioles
Names simple cuboidal epithelium (with Clara/club cells) for terminal bronchioles

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.sc: An arterial blood gas report is shown: pH 7.28, PaCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 28 mEq/L, in a patient with a long-standing history of chronic productive cough and breathlessness.
tk: State the primary acid-base disturbance shown.
State whether metabolic compensation is present, and to what degree.
Name the most likely underlying clinical diagnosis given the history.
Explain the mechanism by which the kidneys compensate for this disturbance.
ck: Correctly identifies respiratory acidosis (low pH, high PaCO2)
Recognizes partial metabolic compensation (elevated HCO3- but pH still low)
Names chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) as the likely diagnosis
Explains renal retention of bicarbonate and increased hydrogen ion excretion over days

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.sc: A chest radiograph is shown with absent lung markings in the left hemithorax, a visible visceral pleural line, and mediastinal shift to the right.
tk: Identify the condition shown on this radiograph.
State whether this presentation, with mediastinal shift, suggests a simple or tension pneumothorax.
Explain the pathophysiological mechanism causing mediastinal shift in this condition.
State the immediate emergency management step for this condition.
ck: Identifies pneumothorax
States mediastinal shift toward the opposite side indicates tension pneumothorax
Explains a one-way valve mechanism causes progressive intrapleural air accumulation, raising pressure and pushing the mediastinum away
States immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion

respiratory/respiratory-histology-acid-b.sc: A summary card compares two patients: one with chronic bronchitis and wheeze, and one with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and dry cough, each with their pulmonary function test values listed.
tk: Classify each patient's underlying pattern as obstructive or restrictive lung disease.
State the expected change in total lung capacity in each pattern.
State the expected change in FEV1/FVC ratio in each pattern.
Name the characteristic histological finding of chronic bronchitis versus pulmonary fibrosis.
ck: Correctly classifies chronic bronchitis as obstructive and pulmonary fibrosis as restrictive
States increased/normal TLC in obstructive disease and decreased TLC in restrictive disease
States decreased FEV1/FVC in obstructive disease and normal/increased FEV1/FVC in restrictive disease
Names mucous gland hyperplasia (Reid index) for chronic bronchitis and interstitial fibrosis/honeycombing for pulmonary fibrosis
